topic: Why monitoring is the bottleneck nobody in industrial AI talks about
draft:
Why monitoring is the bottleneck nobody in industrial AI talks about

Every conversation about AI in manufacturing starts in the wrong place.

Companies want predictive maintenance. Anomaly detection. Autonomous process control. All reasonable goals. The first question they ask is: which model should we use?

Wrong question.

The right question is: do you actually have data? Not indicators. Not KPIs aggregated at 15-minute intervals. Not a dashboard that refreshes when someone clicks. Data — continuous, timestamped, calibrated, stored with enough resolution that a model can reason about it.

Most manufacturers don't. They have a PLC talking to a SCADA system through a protocol that was designed before the internet existed. An operator noting readings on a clipboard. A sensor that fires an alarm when a threshold is crossed but records nothing in between.

There is a concept from mathematics I use every day outside of mathematics: the Laplace transform. When a differential equation is unsolvable in its original domain, you transform the problem into an abstract space where it becomes tractable — solve it there, then transform back. A monitoring system does exactly this. Physical world → sensor → time series → model → actuation. The sensor is the transform.

But if the transform is lossy — if data is batched, dropped, manually entered, or simply not collected — nothing downstream can compensate. You cannot solve in the abstract if your transform is broken.

This is not a metaphor for us. At Auto-Intern, we've been building the transform layer for twelve years, in industries where unmonitored processes quickly become very expensive. What we've learned: the gap is almost never in the AI. It's almost always in the instrument.

We published our full position on this today. Link in the first comment.

If you're planning an AI project for your production environment and you haven't answered the data question first, you're building on air. Happy to talk through what that foundation actually looks like.

The manifesto is live: [link]

One line from it that I keep returning to: 'Critical infrastructure that isn't monitored isn't critical — it's just unexamined risk.'

Question for the room: where have you seen a monitoring gap turn into something expensive — in time, money, or credibility? Factory, server room, home network, research lab — anything goes.

I'll start: we had a customer running a cooling circuit on a production line. No continuous temperature logging — just a high-temp alarm that cut the line. The alarm fired. They assumed sensor glitch, reset it, kept running. Three hours later the line was down for two days. The data that would have shown the gradual drift upward over six hours simply didn't exist.

topic: Dual uplink setup reveal with photo
draft:
15 people, one office, two uplinks.

We put a Debian box between Starlink and DSL, set two default routes by metric, and let Linux handle the failover automatically. When DSL hiccups, nobody in the office notices. No commercial appliance. No configuration wizard. Just iproute2.

We called it AI-heimdall. [photo]

Full config and writeup: [link]

In February, Philipp Lehmann and I added a second internet uplink to the office.

The problem: 15 people, one DSL line, too many simultaneous video calls. The fix: add Starlink as a secondary path and let the routing layer decide which one to use.

Here's how we did it without buying anything expensive:

A Debian rack PC (hostname: AI-heimdall, named after the Norse watchman who sees all nine worlds — a naming tradition started by Odin Holmes) sits between the two uplinks and the internal network. Three interfaces: eno1 for DSL (static IP into the modem), eno2 for Starlink (DHCP), eno4 for the internal network at 10.42.0.0/16.

Two default routes in the main routing table, differentiated by metric. DSL at metric 1001, Starlink at metric 1003. Linux prefers the lower metric. When DSL drops its gateway, that route disappears from the table and traffic flows over Starlink automatically — no manual intervention, no script, no outage visible to anyone in the office.

We also pre-registered two named tables (starlink and dsl) in /etc/iproute2/rt_tables for future policy routing, so we can eventually pin specific traffic — VPN, video calls — to a specific uplink regardless of which is preferred. That's the next step.

A small Python dashboard reads interface stats for both uplinks and displays real-time throughput on a screen in the office. It's also the sanity check: immediately obvious if everything is routing over one link when it shouldn't be.

The actual engineering was in the details: making sure the Starlink DHCP lease doesn't write a competing default route into the main table and displace DSL. Philipp handled the physical installation and integration with the existing backbone; I handled the routing config.

The result: the bottlenecks are gone. More importantly, when DSL has a bad day, nobody in the office notices.

topic: 5 things you only learn at conferences
draft:
Five things you only learn at technical conferences — not from documentation

1. What everyone is actually using vs. what they're publicly recommending
Documentation describes the intended path. Conference hallways describe what actually ships to production. These are often very different.

2. How to calibrate your own skill level
Sitting in a room full of people who've been thinking about your problem longer than you have is uncomfortable and necessary. It's the fastest way to find the ceiling of your current mental model.

3. The names behind the work
Open source is written by people with opinions, constraints, and reasons for their decisions. Meeting them makes the documentation make sense in ways it otherwise doesn't.

4. What the next problem is
The papers describing today's solutions were presented three years ago. Conferences are where you hear about problems that don't have solutions yet — the ones that will define the field in three years.

5. Who to call when you're stuck
A network of people you've had real conversations with is worth more than a list of connections. Conferences build the former.

We've been organising emBO++ in Bochum for eleven years. The best reason to keep running it is still the conversations nobody planned for.

topic: Position paper framing for academic audience
draft:
Auto-Intern Gruppe has published a position paper on the role of monitoring infrastructure in industrial automation and AI deployment: 'If We Can Measure It, You Can Improve It.'

The central argument draws on signal processing principles — specifically domain transformation (analogous to the Laplace transform) — to frame the data pipeline not as auxiliary infrastructure but as the primary epistemological step in any industrial intelligence system.

Key claims relevant to the IIoT and industrial ML literature:
— Aggregated KPI data is not equivalent to continuous sensor data for anomaly detection or predictive modelling
— The retrofit problem (instrumenting existing installed base) is methodologically distinct from greenfield deployment and represents the dominant real-world context
— Proximity between sensing and processing is a physical constraint, not an architectural preference: bandwidth, accuracy, and latency all degrade with distance

Active deployment contexts: large manufacturing, critical infrastructure, defence. Happy to connect with researchers working on time-series data pipelines, industrial anomaly detection, or edge computing architectures.
